# The Department of Lost Sounds

On the morning the church bell disappeared, nobody noticed at first.

The bell had rung at seven every day for a hundred and eleven years. It marked the opening of the bakery, the unlocking of the school gates, and the moment when Mr. Vale, who had retired from the railway in 1986, rose from his chair and announced that he supposed he ought to do something with himself.

That Tuesday, the bell did not ring.

The baker opened late. Three children arrived at school in their pajamas, having slept through their mothers’ calls. Mr. Vale remained in his chair until nearly nine, staring at the window and feeling, without knowing why, that the day had begun improperly.

The bell was still in the tower. The rope still hung beside the stairs. When the vicar pulled it, the great bronze mouth moved back and forth exactly as it should.

No sound came out.

At noon, the vicar telephoned the Department of Lost Sounds.

Mara Bellamy answered on the third ring. She had worked for the department for nineteen years and knew better than to say, “How can I help you?” People who called had usually tried everyone else, and most were embarrassed.

“Department of Lost Sounds,” she said. “What have you lost?”

“A bell,” said the vicar.

“The whole bell?”

“No. Just the sound.”

Mara opened a fresh file.

The department occupied the basement of a municipal building that had once been a public swimming pool. The pool was covered over now, but the tiles remained, pale blue squares beneath the filing cabinets. In damp weather, the room smelled faintly of chlorine and old paper.

There were four employees: Mara; her supervisor, Mr. Chao; a technician named Dev, who repaired the listening equipment; and an intern named Alice, who had applied by mistake and stayed because she liked the work.

They recovered all sorts of sounds. Some were valuable, like the last recording of a singer whose voice had been destroyed in a fire. Some were ordinary: a grandfather’s whistle, a dog’s particular bark, the creak of a stair in a demolished house. Once, they had spent eleven weeks tracking down the noise made by a certain kind of orange wrapping machine, because a woman remembered falling asleep to it while her mother worked the night shift.

Their methods were difficult to explain, partly because Mr. Chao discouraged explanations and partly because the equipment had been assembled from things that should not have worked together. There were microphones, certainly, but also copper wire, tuning forks, a gramophone horn, and a glass jar containing a small amount of seawater.

The jar had belonged to Mr. Chao’s predecessor. Nobody knew what the water did. When Alice asked whether they could remove it and see what happened, Mr. Chao said that was precisely the sort of question that had led to the closing of the old acoustics laboratory.

By two o’clock, Mara and Alice were on the train to the town.

“You’ve never had a church bell before?” Alice asked.

“Not a whole one.”

“What’s the largest sound you’ve recovered?”

“A thunderstorm.”

Alice looked up from her notebook.

“Only part of it,” Mara said. “It had gone missing from a film. The editor remembered the storm being louder when they shot it. He thought someone had altered the recording, but no one had. We found the thunder in a warehouse, caught between two sheets of packing foam.”

“How did it get there?”

“We didn’t ask.”

Alice made a note anyway.

The town was small enough that the station had no ticket barriers and large enough that people argued about whether it was becoming a city. The vicar met them in a green coat and led them uphill past the bakery, where a handwritten sign said SORRY FOR THE LATE START.

Inside the church tower, Mara examined the bell. It was engraved with a date, the names of three donors, and a line from a poem about waking the valley. Its bronze surface bore the soft discolorations of age.

She put her hand against it while the vicar pulled the rope. She felt the vibration travel through her palm and into her wrist. Alice held a microphone beneath the bell, listening through headphones.

“Nothing,” Alice said.

“Any repairs recently?” Mara asked.

“Not to the bell.”

“Has anyone made a recording of it?”

“Of course. Several, I should think. There’s one on the parish website.”

“Does it still sound?”

The vicar hesitated. “I haven’t checked.”

They went downstairs and gathered around his laptop. The parish website had photographs of the church fête, notices about roof repairs, and a video titled *Sunday Bells*. In the video, the tower stood against a blue sky while birds crossed the frame.

The bell moved.

There was no sound.

Alice checked the volume, then played a different video. An advertisement for garden furniture came through the speakers at startling volume.

The vicar closed the laptop.

“That’s rather worse than I expected.”

Mara took a small receiver from her bag and switched it on. A red needle moved across a numbered dial. She walked slowly through the church, stopping at each doorway. Near the font, the needle twitched. Beside the organ, it held steady. At the back door, it swung sharply to the right.

“Something went out this way,” she said.

“Can you tell when?” asked Alice.

“Recently.”

The back door opened onto a narrow lane. Mara followed the needle past bins, a stack of roof tiles, and a wall covered with ivy. At the end of the lane, it settled back to zero.

The bell’s sound had reached the street. After that, it could have gone anywhere.

They spent the afternoon interviewing people. The baker had heard nothing unusual. The school caretaker had noticed that the birds seemed louder than usual, though he admitted he might simply have been listening more carefully. A woman walking a terrier said she had seen a man standing outside the church before dawn, but she described him as “tallish, with a face,” which gave Alice little to write down.

At four, Mara bought tea from a café and spread her notes across a table. Alice drew a map of the streets around the church.

“Could someone have taken it?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Why would they?”

“Sometimes people take things because they don’t know how to ask for them.”

“That sounds very wise.”

“It was in our training manual.”

Alice looked up. Mara smiled.

The training manual was forty years old and mostly concerned with electrical safety. Its only advice on dealing with the public was never to tell a caller that a lost sound had “probably gone for good.” Mr. Chao had underlined the sentence twice.

At the next table, an older man folded his newspaper.

“You’re the people from the council,” he said.

“Not exactly,” said Mara.

“I heard you talking to Mrs. Foster about the bell.”

The man introduced himself as Mr. Vale. He lived across from the church and had heard the bell every morning since his marriage, except for the years he had worked the early shift at the railway.

“My wife used to complain about it,” he said. “Said there was no need to announce seven o’clock to the entire county. But when they stopped it for repairs one summer, she kept waking me to ask the time.”

“When was that?” Mara asked.

“Nineteen ninety-four, perhaps. They had scaffolding up for weeks.”

“Did you hear it yesterday morning?”

“Yes. Same as always.”

“Anything different afterward?”

Mr. Vale thought for a while. “There was a young fellow outside the church. Sat on the wall with his head in his hands. I asked if he was all right, but he didn’t answer.”

“Did you recognize him?”

“No. He had a blue coat, though. Railway blue.”

Alice looked at Mara. The woman with the terrier had mentioned a blue coat too; they had left it out because she had been uncertain whether it was blue or gray.

“Which way did he go?” Mara asked.

“Toward the station. I saw him from my window.”

The stationmaster knew the young man. His name was Lewis, and he had been sleeping in the old waiting room for the past three nights.

“I told him he couldn’t stay,” she said. “But the last train gets in late, and it’s cold. I leave the side door unlocked sometimes.”

“Is he there now?”

“He went out this morning. Left his bag.”

The waiting room had a bench, a radiator that worked unevenly, and a poster advertising a seaside resort whose pier had burned down fifteen years earlier. A canvas bag sat beneath the bench. On top of it lay a blue railway coat, neatly folded.

Mara’s receiver began to hum.

Alice crouched beside the bag. “Should we open it?”

“Not without him.”

The stationmaster made a telephone call. Half an hour later, Lewis arrived carrying a paper cup of soup and a loaf of bread. He stopped in the doorway when he saw them.

The stationmaster explained who they were. Lewis set the soup down very carefully.

“I didn’t steal anything,” he said.

“We haven’t said you did,” Mara replied.

He looked at the bag.

“Can I see what’s inside?” she asked.

He opened it himself. There were clothes, a toothbrush, two paperback books, and a small wooden box. The box had a brass clasp and a crack across the lid.

The receiver’s needle pressed against the end of the dial.

“Where did you get that?” Mara asked.

“It was my mum’s.”

“May I?”

Lewis handed it to her. The box was light. When she opened the clasp, she heard nothing, but the hairs on her arms rose. She closed it again.

“What’s in it?” Alice asked.

“I don’t know,” Lewis said. “It was on her dressing table. She kept earrings in it.”

“Did you take it to the church?”

He nodded.

His mother had died six weeks earlier. He had been clearing her house, working through cupboards and drawers while his older sister handled the paperwork. They had grown up in the town, but he had moved away after school. The house was being sold, and he had come back to collect the last of his things.

“I thought I’d finished,” he said. “Then I found her coat behind the kitchen door. I couldn’t leave it there, but I couldn’t put it in a bag either.”

He had walked out before dawn, carrying the box because it had been in his hand when he left. He sat outside the church until the bell rang.

“When we were kids, she’d open our curtains when it rang,” he said. “Every morning. Even on Saturdays, which we hated.” He rubbed his thumb against the edge of the box. “I sat there thinking I’d forgotten how it sounded. I’d forgotten her voice too. I kept trying to hear either one.”

He had opened the box without thinking. Afterward, he could not remember closing it.

Mara asked if she could take it outside. Lewis followed them onto the platform, where the stationmaster had gone back to her office. A train was due in twelve minutes.

Mara placed the box on the bench and opened the lid.

At first there was only the ordinary noise of the station: a distant engine, wind in the wires, a pigeon moving under the roof. Then a single note emerged, so low that Alice felt it in her ribs before she heard it. The note widened, gathering overtones, until the platform seemed to tremble around them.

The church bell rang once.

Lewis flinched. The sound continued, rolling down the tracks and over the rooftops. People emerged from the station office and the shop across the road. Somewhere uphill, a dog began to bark.

The bell rang a second time, then a third. It gave seven slow strikes before the sound faded.

Alice looked at her watch. It was nearly six.

From the church tower, faint but unmistakable, came another ring. The vicar was trying the rope.

Lewis sat down on the bench. He kept the empty box in his lap.

“I didn’t mean to take it,” he said.

“I know,” said Mara.

“Will it stay there now?”

“I think so. The vicar will call if it doesn’t.”

He ran his fingers over the crack in the lid. “I was hoping I’d hear her when you opened it.”

Mara sat beside him. She had brought a recorder from the department, and for a moment she considered offering to search. But Lewis had not reported a missing voice. His mother’s voice might still be on a telephone message, or a video, or an answering machine in a cupboard. It might return to him unexpectedly while he was washing a plate. The department could not promise any of those things.

“Do you have recordings of her?” she asked.

“My sister does. I haven’t wanted to listen yet.”

The approaching train sounded its horn beyond the bend. Alice moved the equipment off the bench to make room for the passengers gathering on the platform.

“You can keep the box,” Mara said.

Lewis gave a short laugh. “I was going to ask.”

He stayed on the bench after the train arrived. As Mara and Alice boarded, he stood and thanked them. Then he went back into the waiting room to fetch his soup.

On the journey home, Alice wrote up their notes. The bell’s recovery required only a page. She spent longer on Lewis’s account, crossing out several sentences before she was satisfied.

“Do you think the box really took it?” she asked.

“The receiver says it did.”

“I mean, do you think he did it somehow?”

“I don’t know.”

Alice looked out at the fields passing in the dusk. “He wanted to hear something, and then he couldn’t bear to let it go.”

“Perhaps.”

“You don’t have a theory?”

“I have several,” Mara said. “I’ve learned to be careful about putting them in the file.”

Back at the department, Mr. Chao listened to their report and signed the forms. Dev checked the receiver and found a thin coating of bronze-colored dust inside its casing. He collected it in an envelope, labeled it, and put it in a drawer with other substances that had appeared in the equipment over the years.

The next morning, the vicar telephoned.

“The bell rang at seven,” he said. “And I’ve checked the video. It’s back there too.”

“Good,” said Mara.

“There is one small thing. It seems a little louder than before.”

From his tone, she thought he might be pleased about this.

“Give it a few days,” she said. “It may settle.”

That afternoon, a woman called about the sound of rain on her childhood bedroom window. The house had been demolished, and she had found that rain on her current windows did not sound the same. She apologized twice for bothering them.

Mara opened a fresh file and asked what she remembered about the room.

“There was an apple tree outside,” the woman said. “The branches tapped the glass when it was windy. I’d forgotten that until just now.”

Mara wrote it down. They might be able to help; an apple tree changed the sound of rain, and its branches gave them something particular to look for. She asked the woman for the address of the old house and whether she had any photographs.

Across the room, Alice was testing microphones. Dev had taken the seawater jar from the shelf and was wiping dust from beneath it, working carefully so that the water did not spill. The telephone rang again before Mara had finished the call.

It was an ordinary busy afternoon. Somewhere, a sound had gone missing, and someone had begun to describe it.
